cf.title: Print measurements on CTRL-C in pgbench

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and the idea fits pgbench as a core tool. Three fixable points remain: already-exists-1 asks why `-T` with `-P` falls short, standards-compat-1 shows that exit(130) lets a calling shell loop continue, and maintenance-fit-2 notes that Windows behaviour is undefined. The author calls the patch a POC and leaves the exit code open in message #1, so these are open design points and do not count against the goal.

brief.title: pgbench: print partial results on first Ctrl-C
brief.problem: Developers run pgbench for a few seconds, press Ctrl-C, change code and run again. Today Ctrl-C kills pgbench and prints none of the statistics collected so far.
brief.proposed_design: On the first SIGINT, pgbench stops starting new transactions, discards in-flight ones, prints the usual summary with the existing "Run was aborted" message, and exits with status 130. A second SIGINT uses the default handler and kills the process at once. All waits are capped at one second (MAX_IDLE_WAIT_USEC) so a thread idle in \sleep notices the signal.
user_visible_surface: Ctrl-C (SIGINT) now prints the run summary instead of killing pgbench silently.
Exit status 130 after a first SIGINT.
\sleep and other waits now wake at least once per second.
author_claims: Useful for short manual runs that compare performance before and after a code change.
Reviewer Kirill Reshke is +1 on the UX and on the double Ctrl-C behaviour.
v2 fixes a race where workers could send new commands after the stop flag was set.
brief.thread_state: Kirill Reshke reviewed v1, found a race in the stop-flag check, and pointed to the earlier thread "Make pgbench exit on SIGINT more reliably" for Windows handling. The author posted v2 with the fix; the exit code and Windows behaviour are still open.
unclear: The material does not say how the patch behaves on Windows, where signal handling differs.
The proposal does not say whether status 130 is the right exit code; the author is unsure himself.
No documentation hunk is included, so the pgbench docs on SIGINT and exit status are unchanged.
The patch does not say how discarded in-flight transactions affect latency, TPS and per-script statistics in the summary.
The thread gives no measurement of overhead from waking every second during long \sleep periods.

objections.title: Existing -T and -P options already cover short manual runs
objections.failure_scenario: A developer who wants a 5-10 second comparison can run `pgbench -T 10 -P 1` and get the full summary plus per-second TPS and latency. The patch adds a new SIGINT path, a new exit status and a one-second wait cap that every pgbench run then carries. The open Windows question has to be resolved and maintained for a case these options already handle.
objections.argument: Message #1 describes runs of a known short length ("5-10 seconds"). That is the use case for `-T`, which ends with the normal summary, and `-P` prints TPS and latency while the run is going, so a user who presses Ctrl-C has already seen the numbers. The proposal does not mention either option or say why they fall short. Without that, the gain looks like convenience: no need to choose the duration in advance. A committer would likely ask whether that convenience is worth the permanent signal-handling code.
objections.author_must_show: What does a Ctrl-C summary give that `-T` with `-P 1` does not, for the short comparison runs described in message #1?

critic.reasoning: `-T 10 -P 1` gives the numbers for the 5-10 second runs in message #1, and the thread does not say why that falls short. One +1 in message #2 does not show the need is common.

objections.title: Exit 130 instead of re-raising SIGINT breaks shell loop interruption
objections.failure_scenario: A user runs pgbench inside a bash loop or a Makefile, for example for each scale factor, and presses Ctrl-C. Bash sees pgbench exit normally with status 130 rather than die from SIGINT, so it keeps going and starts the next pgbench run. The user has to press Ctrl-C again for every remaining iteration.
objections.argument: Today pgbench dies from SIGINT, and calling shells rely on that to stop the whole script. The usual convention for programs that catch SIGINT is to clean up, reset the handler and re-raise the signal, not to exit(130). The author says in message #1 that the exit code is still open. The patch adds no documentation hunk, so the documented exit statuses, 0, 1 and 2 with partial results, would gain an undocumented fourth value.
objections.author_must_show: After printing the summary, will pgbench re-raise SIGINT so calling shells see a signal death, and how will the exit-status documentation change?

critic.reasoning: Bash continues a loop when the child catches SIGINT and exits normally, even with status 130, so the scenario is real. The author leaves the exit code open in message #1, and the patch has no documentation hunk for the new status.

objections.title: Windows behaviour left undefined for a cross-platform tool
objections.failure_scenario: A Windows user presses Ctrl-C during a run. pgbench may print nothing, print a summary while threads keep running, or hang until a wait expires. The user finds out only on that platform, and the bug report then goes to a committer who has no Windows setup.
objections.argument: Windows delivers console Ctrl-C through a separate handler thread rather than POSIX SIGINT, so a design built on signal state and EINTR does not carry over unchanged. Message #2 points to an earlier thread on exactly this issue, and message #3 only promises to read it. The touched files list only pgbench.c, with no tests and no documentation for either platform.
objections.author_must_show: What does a first and a second Ctrl-C do on Windows with v2, and how does a test show that it matches the Unix behaviour?

critic.reasoning: Windows runs the SIGINT handler in a separate thread and has no EINTR, and the thread does not say what v2 does there. Message #3 only promises to read the earlier thread, so the question is open.

refuted.title: Stop-flag checks spread through the client state machine
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a new state or wait path to advanceConnectionState() and does not check aborted_by_sigint. After the first Ctrl-C, that path sends more commands to the server and those transactions still count in the summary. Nobody notices, because no test fails.
refuted.argument: Message #2 found exactly this bug in v1, where the flag was checked once per threadRun loop and a worker could run a full state-machine pass after it was set. v2 moves the check before advanceConnectionState() (message #3), but the design still depends on every future path honouring the flag. The proposal does not say how the stop is enforced in one place, or which test would catch a missed check.
refuted.author_must_show: Where is the single point that stops new commands after the first SIGINT, and which TAP test fails if a new code path skips it?

critic.reasoning: Message #3 says v2 checks the flag before the call to advanceConnectionState(), so a state added inside that function is already behind the check. The remaining request for a TAP test is below level 2.

refuted.title: Demand rests on one workflow that -T and -P already cover
refuted.failure_scenario: A developer who wants a 5-10 second comparison can run `pgbench -T 10`, or add `-P 1` to see per-second TPS and latency before pressing Ctrl-C. If the patch goes in for this case alone, every pgbench run carries the new SIGINT path and the one-second wait cap, which mostly serves users who already have these options.
refuted.argument: The only demand shown is the author's own loop in message #1, plus one +1 in message #2 that calls it a UX improvement for manual testing. The thread does not say why `-T` or `-P` falls short for this workflow, and gives no -hackers, -general or -bugs reports of users who lost results to Ctrl-C. The cost is small but shared: changed exit status, a cap on \sleep waits, and Windows handling still open in message #3.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users interrupt pgbench runs they could not bound with -T or watch with -P, and what do they lose today without the summary?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which makes the same `-T` and `-P` argument with a more concrete question for the author.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Exit 130 instead of re-raising SIGINT breaks shell loop interruption

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a SIGINT path, a new exit status and a one-second wait cap in pgbench.c, with Windows handling still open.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: `pgbench -T 10 -P 1` already gives a summary and per-second numbers for the short runs in message #1.

questions: What does a Ctrl-C summary give that `-T` with `-P 1` does not, for the short comparison runs described in message #1?
After printing the summary, will pgbench reset the handler and re-raise SIGINT so a calling shell loop or Makefile stops, or exit with status 130?
What do a first and a second Ctrl-C do on Windows with v2?
How do the discarded in-flight transactions affect the TPS, latency and per-script numbers in the summary?
How will the pgbench documentation on exit status and interrupted runs change?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows pgbench's thread and wait loop and frontend signal handling, including Windows console Ctrl-C handling.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the SIGINT path in pgbench on every platform, the exit-status contract that scripts will depend on, and the one-second wait cap, for as long as pgbench ships.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 two days after the review in message #2 and said he will read the earlier Windows thread.

priority.reason: The patch is about 4.6 KB in one file and serves developers who run pgbench by hand, though the thread shows only one such workflow. The exit behaviour and the Windows behaviour need an answer before code review is useful.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check how v2 handles in-flight transactions in the statistics, whether the handler is async-signal-safe, or how the one-second wait cap interacts with `-R` and `\sleep`.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Extend pgbench partitioning to pgbench_history
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pgbench's --partitions option also partition pgbench_history, using the same method as pgbench_accounts. It adds no separate option to turn this on or off.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not answer Melanie Plageman's review for about three months, so Robert Haas returned the entry with feedback. She asked why the history table should be partitioned by account ID rather than by time, and why tellers and branches were left out. She also said the doc text wrongly implies that the pgbench_history partitions are created with equal sizes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since there has been no response to these review comments for more
than 3 months, I have set https://commitfest.postgresql.org/48/4679/
to Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgbench --continue-on-error: clarify TPS and failure reporting
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch rewords the pgbench documentation for --continue-on-error so it states that failed transactions are reported separately and are not counted in TPS. A second paragraph describes when the main report's latency average includes failed transactions, which depends on --progress, --rate and --latency-limit.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Reviewers agreed with the TPS wording, the latency wording went through one round of revision, and the thread ends with the author posting v2 with no further reply and no objection.

precedents_retrieved.summary:

Reverted commit(s): Hack pg_ctl to report postmaster's exit status.

This reverts commit 6a5084eed49552bfc8859c438c8d74ad09fc5d3f.
We learned what we needed to know from that.

precedents_retrieved.title: tablesync early exit
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes a tablesync worker call process_syncing_tables() before it enters the apply main loop, so a worker with nothing left to do exits early. The author presented it as a small optimization and as a cleaner split of work between tablesync and apply workers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila objected that exiting before the tablesync worker receives any message skips changes up to the LSN where the copy finished. That is safe with the current code but would lose changes for the table in a design where the apply worker applies streamed in-progress transactions, which had already been proposed on -hackers. The saving was only the work to receive messages for one transaction, so the author withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As per my understanding, this is safe as per the current code but it
can't be guaranteed for future implementations and the amount of extra
work is additional work to receive the messages for one transaction.

precedents_retrieved.title: Exit walsender before confirming remote flush in logical replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a logical replication walsender exit at shutdown without waiting for the subscriber to confirm flush of all sent WAL, so that a publisher with a large time-delayed apply can still stop. Later versions add an optional SHUTDOWN_MODE clause ('wait_flush' or 'immediate') to START_REPLICATION for logical replication.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown messages, about a month before the decision, still discuss whether the option should be a boolean or a mode with an explicit default, and they contain minor review comments on v7-0002.

precedents_retrieved.title: Do not exit on postmaster death event inside CRIT sections.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes a process that detects postmaster death inside WaitEventSetWait defer its exit while it is in a critical section, and exit only after the section ends. The goal was to stop proc_exit(1) from releasing LWLocks mid-change, which let the checkpointer flush a modified buffer whose WAL record was never written.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that deferring exit leads to systems that fail to shut down. The author then confirmed that the checkpointer waits forever in LWLockAcquire in the test. Tom also argued that proc_exit(1) after postmaster death is the real defect, and that removing the death check is as hazardous as keeping it this late in the v18 cycle. The thread instead reverted commit bc22dc0e0, which had started using condition variables inside critical sections, and left better postmaster-death handling to a new thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I do not like this patch one bit: it will replace one set of problems with another set, namely systems that fail to shut down.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgbench allow '=' in \set
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Tom Lane, Pavel Stehule
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch let pgbench ignore a leading '=' in a \set expression, so a script could write `\set id = 1 + ...` for readability. Later in the thread ':=' was suggested as an alternative separator.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected to optional noise words because they can create parser ambiguities later, as `LOCK TABLE foo` versus `LOCK foo` did, and because '=' only restates what `\set` already says. Tom Lane and Pavel Stehule had raised consistency concerns with pgbench itself and with psql. The author then marked the entry rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Generally, I don't like optional noise words.

precedents_retrieved.title: merging pgbench logs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pgbench option, -m/--merge-logs, that merges the per-thread transaction log files into one file after the run ends. It uses a 2-way merge on the time field and supports --rate, --aggregate-interval and --latency-limit log formats.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Fabien COELHO, the reviewer, argued that a post-run merge belongs in an external script, and that the merge code was too heavy: it re-reads files repeatedly (p²n I/O) and duplicates parsing and printing for each log format. He proposed that threads write one shared log file directly and that the feature be skipped under thread emulation. Tomas Vondra declined because a shared file does not work for the aggregated log and he would not add a feature that fails with --disable-thread-safety. The thread ended in May 2015 without a revised patch or an agreed design.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: My view is that you're code is on the too-heavy side, and adds a burden for later maintenance for rather a should-be-simple feature, really just so it works for "thread emulation" that probably nought people use or really need.

precedents_retrieved.title: Skip collecting decoded changes of already-aborted transactions
precedents_retrieved.summary: Logical decoding checks CLOG when it first decodes a transaction and stops collecting decoded changes for transactions already known to be aborted, so large aborted transactions are not decoded again after a restart or lag. After Andres Freund's review, the revised patch checks transaction status only for large transactions at eviction time.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The revised patch did not compile because `logical_replication_mode` was undeclared in `ReorderBufferCheckTXNAbort`. The author posted no new version after this report, so the CF manager returned the entry with feedback. Andres Freund's earlier concerns, misuse of TransactionIdDidAbort() and slow CLOG lookups, were addressed in the design but not decisive.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With no update to the thread and the compilation still failing I'm
marking this as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert refactoring of restore command code to shell_restore.c
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert refactoring of restore command code to shell_restore.c
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits 24c35ec and 57169ad.  PreRestoreCommand() and
PostRestoreCommand() need to be put closer to the system() call calling
a restore_command, as they enable in_restore_command for the startup
process which would in turn trigger an immediate proc_exit() in the
SIGTERM handler.  Perhaps we could get rid of this behavior entirely,
but 24c35ec has made the window where the flag is enabled much larger
than it was, and any Postgres-like actions (palloc, etc.) taken by code
paths while the flag is enabled could lead to more severe issues in the
shutdown processing.

Note that curculio has showed that there are much more problems in this
area, unrelated to this change, actually, hence the issues related to
that had better be addressed first.  Keeping the code of HEAD in line
with the stable branches should make that a bit easier.

Per discussion with Andres Freund and Nathan Bossart.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".
Reverted commit(s): Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process.; Fix segmentation fault that commit ac22929a26 caused.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Revert ac22929a26, as well as the followup fix 113d3591b8. Because it broke
the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict
on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled
in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(). It caused, for example,
SIGHUP signal handler or walreceiver process to wake that startup process
up unnecessarily frequently.

Additionally, add the comments about why that dedicated latch that
the reverted patch tried to get rid of should not be removed.

Thanks to Kyotaro Horiguchi for the discussion.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found; the corpus search returned no earlier attempt at the same or a similar idea. Message #2 points to an earlier thread, "Make pgbench exit on SIGINT more reliably", but only as possible context on Windows handling, with no outcome or rejection reason, so no earlier objection can be checked against this proposal.

Beyond the exit-status contract, nothing else in this angle seems to need an objection. The proposal adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object or dump format. It reuses the existing 'Run was aborted' message, so scripts can tell partial output apart from a normal result.

The patch changes only client-side signal handling in src/bin/pgbench/pgbench.c. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog entry, wire protocol message or server ABI change. Discarded in-flight transactions close as an ordinary client disconnect, so the server rolls them back, which is existing behaviour. This angle has nothing to object to.

The proposal changes only how the pgbench client handles SIGINT in its own process. It grants no privilege, exposes no data, and touches no server code, authentication or connection setup. Any change in server-side work after Ctrl-C stays within what the same user could already do with the same connection.

From the maintenance angle the idea fits core: pgbench is a core tool, the change touches one file and costs nothing on the server. The one-second wait cap adds a negligible wakeup cost, so it is not raised.
Only one objection from this angle. No extension or external tool replaces the feature, and no precedent applies.
The likely user group is wider than one person, since many people press Ctrl-C on pgbench. The thread does not show this, so the objection asks for evidence and does not argue against the idea.
